newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil states debt scandal hits Central Bank.
newsitem.headline: Brazil states debt scandal hits Central Bank.

text.p: A probe by Brazilian legislators into a multi-million dollar scam involving state and city bonds was set to widen Wednesday after the government's financial watchdog launched an investigation into the Central Bank.

A spokesman for the Federal Accounts Tribunal (TCU) said the body would audit the Central Bank's procedures for authorizing bond issues by states and cities to see whether there had been "errors or omissions".
"We consider this an unusual step for the TCU to take," TCU spokesman Marcos Santos said.

A special Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry (CPI) has been set up by the Senate to investigate allegations that brokers and officials may have siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars through suspect issues of up to $6.0 billion in municipal bonds.

The allegations, billed as potentially one of the biggest scandals to rock Brazilian politics since the downfall of former president Fernando Collor de Mello, center on claims states and cities sold debt at well below market prices, ensuring instant profits for brokerages involved in the scam.
Last week, the Central Bank shut down more than a dozen brokerages and small banks suspected of involvement.
A Central Bank spokesman said the bank was not concerned by the TCU investigation because it had advised against authorizing the suspect securities issues.
Government-allied senators leading the CPI probe have vowed to pursue their investigations all the way to the "big fish".
The CPI may even grant the middlemen amnesty in order to encourage them to reveal the names of the ringleaders.

"The most dangerous thing would be to let the really guilty ones get off scot-free," Senator Esperidiao Amin, who first suggested the idea of an amnesty for the small fry, told the media in a flurry of television and radio interviews Tuesday.
An aide to Senator Vilson Kleinubing said the CPI might eventually question the governors of Pernambuco, Santa Catarina and Alagoas states, as well as senior officials of Sao Paulo city.

Later on Wednesday, the panel was due to go into an all-night session gathering testimony from current and former financial officers from the state of Pernambuco and from three municipalities in Sao Paulo state.

The debt scandal is complex. In addition to allegations that public money was diverted to secret accounts abroad, in particular in Paraguay, investigators say state officials lied to the Central Bank and the Senate about their financing needs.

Under Brazil's constitution, states can only raise money in the market to pay court settlements. Senators say the states in question exaggerated the settlements they had to pay, even falsifying documents, and used the excess to cover normal day-to-day expenditures.
